A Convex Splitting Spectral Method for the Phase Field Crystal Equation: Energy Stability, Computational Stability Maps, and Three-Dimensional GPU Simulations

Saulo Orizaga Email: saulo.orizaga@nmt.edu Address: Department of Mathematics, New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology, 801 Leroy Place, Socorro, NM 87801, USA    Peimeng Yin Email: pyin@utep.edu Address: Department of Mathematical Sciences, The University of Texas at El Paso, 500 W University Ave, El Paso, TX 79968, USA    Deep Choudhuri Email: deep.choudhuri@nmt.edu Address: Department of Materials and Metallurgical Engineering, New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology, 801 Leroy Place, Socorro, NM 87801, USA
Abstract

We present an efficient Fourier spectral method based on the convex splitting framework of Eyre [1] for the phase field crystal (PFC) equation. The proposed first-order scheme is unconditionally energy stable and conserves mass to machine precision. An energy stability theorem is established using a truncated potential argument, and a semi-analytical neutral stability curve is derived from a dominant-mode energy balance, providing a closed-form characterization of the practical stability boundary. The classical sufficient condition a≥2a\geq 2 is shown to be conservative: a computational stability map obtained from 40,000 GPU-accelerated PFC simulations reveals that energy-stable solutions persist for values of aa significantly below this threshold. Crucially, accuracy analysis demonstrates that smaller values of aa within the stable region consistently yield lower L2L^{2} errors. This high-fidelity regime is rigorously verified through an extended asymptotic stress test consisting of a long-time three-dimensional simulation on a 2563256^{3} grid up to Tf=10,000T_{f}=10,000, successfully executing 10610^{6} continuous temporal increments deep within the relaxed stability regime, well below the classical convex splitting limit (a<2a<2), while preserving strict monotonic energy dissipation and machine-precision mass conservation. Finally, two-dimensional and three-dimensional simulations at resolutions up to 5123512^{3} are performed on a single consumer GPU, demonstrating the scalability of the proposed framework for resolving complex phase-field dynamics without requiring HPC infrastructure. The code is made publicly available on GitHub.11 1 GitHub: https://github.com/sauloorizaga/CS-PFC.

Keywords: 
Phase field crystal equation , convex splitting , energy stability , GPU computing , spectral methods

1 Introduction

The phase field crystal (PFC) equation is a sixth-order nonlinear parabolic PDE that effectively captures microstructure evolution at atomic length and diffusive time scales [2, 3]. This model bridges the gap between atomistic simulations and classical phase field models [4], finding applications in grain growth, spinodal decomposition, liquid phase epitaxial growth, and crack propagation [2, 3, 5, 6]. The PFC equation takes the form

ϕt=Δ​μ,μ=(Δ+1)2​ϕ−r​ϕ+ϕ3,\phi_{t}=\Delta\mu,\qquad\mu=(\Delta+1)^{2}\phi-r\phi+\phi^{3},

where ϕ\phi is the atomistic density field and r>0r>0 is the undercooling parameter. The PFC equation belongs to a broader class of phase-field models capable of producing rich microphase morphologies, including lamellar, hexagonal, and spherical structures. Similar morphological diversity is observed in block copolymer (BCP) models [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12], where the competition between short-range and long-range interactions governs the emergent microstructure.

Numerical methods for the PFC equation have been extensively studied. Early contributions include the spectral approach of Cheng and Warren [13] and the unconditionally stable finite difference framework of Wise, Wang and Lowengrub [6]. Finite element methods were proposed in [14], while isogeometric analysis frameworks were developed in [5, 15]. Splitting schemes and energy-stable time integrators for phase-field models have been studied extensively in the literature [16, 17, 18]. Higher-order temporal schemes including BDF2–CS were established by Glasner and Orizaga [19], which demonstrated that convex splitting provides a robust and accurate framework for both the Cahn–Hilliard and PFC equations in two spatial dimensions. GPU-accelerated pseudo-spectral methods for phase-field equations were pioneered by Shen and collaborators [20], whose framework directly inspired the GPU implementation of [21] for the Cahn–Hilliard equation and is extended here to three-dimensional PFC simulations on consumer hardware.

More recently, significant advances in energy-stable discretizations for the PFC equation have been reported. Shin, Lee and Lee [22] developed high-order convex splitting Runge–Kutta methods using Fourier spectral discretization, establishing unconditional energy stability and unique solvability for second and third-order temporal schemes, with long-time simulations restricted to two spatial dimensions. Yang and Han [23] proposed linearly first- and second-order unconditionally energy stable schemes for the PFC model. Gomez and Nogueira [5] presented an unconditionally energy-stable second-order method using isogeometric analysis, with three-dimensional validation at N=1283N=128^{3} resolution. Most recently, Saylor, Horváth and Sharma [24] proposed a first-order convex splitting hybridizable/embedded discontinuous Galerkin (HDG/EDG) finite element method for the PFC equation, establishing unconditional energy stability and existence and uniqueness of the discrete solution. While theoretically rigorous, that approach requires rewriting the sixth-order equation as a system of seven coupled first-order equations, four stabilization parameters, and large-scale finite element libraries such as MFEM, PETSc, and MUMPS. Notably, three-dimensional simulations could be expensive. More recently, the scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) approaches [25, 26] have provided an alternative framework for unconditionally stable discretizations of gradient flow equations. While significant progress has been made in these directions, the present work returns to the classical convex splitting framework and addresses the long-standing question of the practical stability threshold for the splitting parameter aa, which will be specified in Section 3.

These observations directly motivate the present contribution. We present a simple and efficient Fourier spectral method based on the convex splitting framework of Eyre [1]. The proposed method is unconditionally energy stable and conserves mass to machine precision. A central contribution of this work is a computational stability analysis of the splitting parameter aa, performed via GPU-accelerated parameter sweeps involving 40,000 independent PFC simulations. Our results reveal that the classical stability threshold a≥2a\geq 2 is sufficient but not sharp: a semi-analytical neutral stability curve derived from a dominant-mode energy balance provides a closed-form characterization of the practical stability boundary, and accuracy analysis demonstrates that smaller values of aa within the stable region consistently yield lower L2L^{2} errors. The spectral framework scales naturally to three dimensions via GPU acceleration, with fully resolved simulations demonstrated on grids of 1283128^{3}, 2563256^{3}, and 5123512^{3}, the latter on a single consumer GPU, requiring no HPC infrastructure. Two-dimensional simulations on 256×256256\times 256 grids are also presented. To the best of our knowledge, spectral simulations of the PFC equation at 5123512^{3} resolution have not been previously reported in the literature.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the mathematical model. Section 3 introduces the convex splitting scheme and its spectral discretization. Section 4 establishes unconditional energy stability, mass conservation, and uniqueness of the discrete solution. Section 5 presents the computational stability analysis, including the semi-analytical neutral stability curve and the GPU-accelerated stability map. Section 6 presents the accuracy analysis for multiple initial conditions. Section 7 presents two-dimensional simulations including crystal growth, morphological diversity, and grain boundary dynamics. Section 8 presents three-dimensional GPU-accelerated simulations at resolutions up to 5123512^{3}. Conclusions are drawn in Section 9.

1.1 Comparison with Hybridizable/Embedded Discontinuous Galerkin Methods

The recent work of Saylor, Horváth and Sharma [24] and the present contribution share a common foundation: both employ a first-order convex splitting temporal discretization for the PFC equation with unconditional energy stability. Despite this shared framework, the two approaches differ substantially in complexity and scalability. Saylor et al. [24] treat the nonlinear term implicitly via Newton iterations and rewrite the sixth-order equation as a system of seven coupled equations, requiring large-scale libraries such as MFEM, PETSc, and MUMPS, with three-dimensional simulations not demonstrated. The present spectral scheme treats the nonlinear term explicitly, operates directly on the sixth-order equation, requires no external libraries, and scales naturally to three dimensions via GPU acceleration at resolutions up to 5123512^{3} on a single consumer GPU. The two approaches are therefore complementary: while the HDG/EDG framework of [24] offers rigorous theoretical foundations and flexibility for complex geometries and boundary conditions, the proposed spectral method prioritizes simplicity, GPU-nativity, and accessibility on consumer hardware without HPC infrastructure.

2 Mathematical Model

The phase field crystal (PFC) equation derives from the gradient flow in H−1H^{-1} of the Swift–Hohenberg free energy functional

E⁡[ϕ]=∫Ω(14​ϕ4+1−r2​ϕ2−|∇ϕ|2+12​(Δ​ϕ)2)​𝑑x,E[\phi]=\int_{\Omega}\left(\frac{1}{4}\phi^{4}+\frac{1-r}{2}\phi^{2}-|\nabla\phi|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(\Delta\phi)^{2}\right)dx, (1)

where ϕ\phi is the atomistic density field and r>0r>0 is the undercooling parameter. The governing equation reads

ϕt=Δ​μ,μ=ϕ3+(1−r)​ϕ+2​Δ​ϕ+Δ2​ϕ.\phi_{t}=\Delta\mu,\qquad\mu=\phi^{3}+(1-r)\phi+2\Delta\phi+\Delta^{2}\phi. (2)

Under suitable boundary conditions (e.g., homogeneous Dirichlet, homogeneous Neumann, or periodic boundary conditions), the PFC equation admits the following energy dissipation law:

d​Ed​t=−‖∇μ‖2≤0.\frac{dE}{dt}=-\|\nabla\mu\|^{2}\leq 0.

3 The Convex Splitting Scheme

Following Eyre [1] and [19], we decompose the free energy E=E++E−E=E^{+}+E^{-} where

E+​(ϕ)=∫Ω1−r+a2​ϕ2+12​(Δ​ϕ)2​𝑑x,E−​(ϕ)=∫Ω14​ϕ4−a2​ϕ2−|∇ϕ|2​𝑑x,E^{+}(\phi)=\int_{\Omega}\frac{1-r+a}{2}\phi^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(\Delta\phi)^{2}\,dx,\qquad E^{-}(\phi)=\int_{\Omega}\frac{1}{4}\phi^{4}-\frac{a}{2}\phi^{2}-|\nabla\phi|^{2}\,dx, (3)

where a>0a>0 is the splitting parameter. The term 14​ϕ4−a2​ϕ2\frac{1}{4}\phi^{4}-\frac{a}{2}\phi^{2} is concave provided a≥3​‖ϕ‖L∞2a\geq 3\|\phi\|^{2}_{L^{\infty}}, which holds in practice for a≥2a\geq 2 [19].

Treating E+E^{+} implicitly and E−E^{-} explicitly yields the first-order convex splitting scheme:

ϕn+1−ϕnΔ​t=Δ​μn+1,\frac{\phi^{n+1}-\phi^{n}}{\Delta t}=\Delta\mu^{n+1}, (4)
μn+1=(1−r+a)​ϕn+1+Δ2​ϕn+1+(ϕn)3−a​ϕn−2​Δ​ϕn.\mu^{n+1}=(1-r+a)\phi^{n+1}+\Delta^{2}\phi^{n+1}+(\phi^{n})^{3}-a\phi^{n}-2\Delta\phi^{n}. (5)

In the Fourier spectral discretization, the scheme admits the efficient closed-form update

ϕ^n+1​(𝐤)=ϕ^n+Δ​t​(−|𝐤|2​[(ϕn)3−a​ϕn]^+2​|𝐤|4​ϕ^n)1+Δ​t​((1−r+a)​|𝐤|2+|𝐤|6),\hat{\phi}^{n+1}(\mathbf{k})=\frac{\hat{\phi}^{n}+\Delta t\left(-|\mathbf{k}|^{2}\widehat{\left[(\phi^{n})^{3}-a\phi^{n}\right]}+2|\mathbf{k}|^{4}\hat{\phi}^{n}\right)}{1+\Delta t\left((1-r+a)|\mathbf{k}|^{2}+|\mathbf{k}|^{6}\right)}, (6)

where ⋅^\hat{\cdot} denotes the discrete Fourier transform. Standard pseudo-spectral methods are used for the spatial discretization [27], requiring no linear solvers or iterative methods.

4 Scheme Properties

Theorem 1 (Mass Conservation).

The convex splitting scheme (4) conserves mass exactly for all Δ​t>0\Delta t>0:

∫Ωϕn+1​𝑑x=∫Ωϕn​𝑑x,∀n≥0.\int_{\Omega}\phi^{n+1}\,dx=\int_{\Omega}\phi^{n}\,dx,\qquad\forall n\geq 0.
Proof.

Integrating (4) over Ω\Omega and applying the divergence theorem with periodic boundary conditions:

1Δ​t​∫Ω(ϕn+1−ϕn)​𝑑x=∫ΩΔ​μn+1​𝑑x=∮∂Ω∇μn+1⋅𝐧​𝑑s=0.\frac{1}{\Delta t}\int_{\Omega}(\phi^{n+1}-\phi^{n})\,dx=\int_{\Omega}\Delta\mu^{n+1}\,dx=\oint_{\partial\Omega}\nabla\mu^{n+1}\cdot\mathbf{n}\,ds=0.

∎

Remark 1 (Spectral Verification).

In the Fourier spectral discretization, mass conservation holds to machine precision since the zero wavenumber mode ϕ^​(𝟎)\hat{\phi}(\mathbf{0}) is unchanged by the scheme, the right-hand side vanishes identically at 𝐤=𝟎\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{0}. This is confirmed numerically in all simulations presented in Section 7.

Remark 2 (Existence and Uniqueness).

Existence and uniqueness of the discrete solution follow from the strictly convex structure of the implicit part of the scheme (4), as established in  [19] for both the Cahn–Hilliard and PFC equations.

To establish unconditional energy stability for the sixth-order system, we adopt a truncated potential argument following the mathematical framework of Shen et al. [28]. This approach ensures global concavity of the expansive energy components, yielding the following result:

Theorem 2 (Unconditional Energy Stability).

Let Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a periodic domain and let ϕn∈Hper2​(Ω)\phi^{n}\in H^{2}_{\mathrm{per}}(\Omega). Define a truncated potential FM∈C2​(ℝ)F_{M}\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}) satisfying

FM​(ϕ)=14​ϕ4for ​|ϕ|≤M,F_{M}(\phi)=\frac{1}{4}\phi^{4}\quad\text{for }|\phi|\leq M,

and

|FM′′​(ϕ)|≤LM,∀ϕ∈ℝ.|F_{M}^{\prime\prime}(\phi)|\leq L_{M},\qquad\forall\phi\in\mathbb{R}.

Let fM=FM′f_{M}=F_{M}^{\prime} and define the modified energy functional

EM​(ϕ)=∫Ω[FM​(ϕ)+1−r2​ϕ2−|∇ϕ|2+12​(Δ​ϕ)2]​𝑑x.E_{M}(\phi)=\int_{\Omega}\left[F_{M}(\phi)+\frac{1-r}{2}\phi^{2}-|\nabla\phi|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(\Delta\phi)^{2}\right]dx.

Decompose

EM​(ϕ)=EM+​(ϕ)+EM−​(ϕ),E_{M}(\phi)=E_{M}^{+}(\phi)+E_{M}^{-}(\phi),

where

EM+​(ϕ)=∫Ω[1−r+a2​ϕ2+12​(Δ​ϕ)2]​𝑑x,E_{M}^{+}(\phi)=\int_{\Omega}\left[\frac{1-r+a}{2}\phi^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(\Delta\phi)^{2}\right]dx,

and

EM−​(ϕ)=∫Ω[FM​(ϕ)−a2​ϕ2−|∇ϕ|2]​𝑑x.E_{M}^{-}(\phi)=\int_{\Omega}\left[F_{M}(\phi)-\frac{a}{2}\phi^{2}-|\nabla\phi|^{2}\right]dx.

Assume

a≥LM,1−r+a>0.a\geq L_{M},\qquad 1-r+a>0.

Consider the convex splitting scheme

ϕn+1−ϕnΔ​t=Δ​μn+1,\frac{\phi^{n+1}-\phi^{n}}{\Delta t}=\Delta\mu^{n+1}, (2.1)

with chemical potential

μn+1=(1−r+a)​ϕn+1+Δ2​ϕn+1+fM​(ϕn)−a​ϕn−2​Δ​ϕn.\mu^{n+1}=(1-r+a)\phi^{n+1}+\Delta^{2}\phi^{n+1}+f_{M}(\phi^{n})-a\phi^{n}-2\Delta\phi^{n}. (2.2)

Then the numerical solution satisfies the discrete energy law

EM​(ϕn+1)+1Δ​t​‖ϕn+1−ϕn‖H−12≤EM​(ϕn),∀Δ​t>0.E_{M}(\phi^{n+1})+\frac{1}{\Delta t}\|\phi^{n+1}-\phi^{n}\|_{H^{-1}}^{2}\leq E_{M}(\phi^{n}),\qquad\forall\Delta t>0.
Proof.

The second variation of EM+E_{M}^{+} is

δ2​EM+​(ϕ)​[v,v]=∫Ω[(1−r+a)​v2+(Δ​v)2]​𝑑x.\delta^{2}E_{M}^{+}(\phi)[v,v]=\int_{\Omega}\left[(1-r+a)v^{2}+(\Delta v)^{2}\right]dx.

Since 1−r+a>01-r+a>0,

δ2​EM+​(ϕ)​[v,v]≥0,\delta^{2}E_{M}^{+}(\phi)[v,v]\geq 0,

and therefore EM+E_{M}^{+} is strictly convex.

Next, the second variation of EM−E_{M}^{-} is

δ2​EM−​(ϕ)​[v,v]=∫Ω[(FM′′​(ϕ)−a)​v2−2​|∇v|2]​𝑑x.\delta^{2}E_{M}^{-}(\phi)[v,v]=\int_{\Omega}\left[(F_{M}^{\prime\prime}(\phi)-a)v^{2}-2|\nabla v|^{2}\right]dx.

Because

FM′′​(ϕ)≤LM≤a,F_{M}^{\prime\prime}(\phi)\leq L_{M}\leq a,

we obtain

(FM′′​(ϕ)−a)​v2≤0.(F_{M}^{\prime\prime}(\phi)-a)v^{2}\leq 0.

Hence

δ2​EM−​(ϕ)​[v,v]≤0,\delta^{2}E_{M}^{-}(\phi)[v,v]\leq 0,

which proves that EM−E_{M}^{-} is globally concave.

Take the H−1H^{-1} inner product of (2.1) with ϕn+1−ϕn\phi^{n+1}-\phi^{n}:

⟨ϕn+1−ϕnΔ​t,ϕn+1−ϕn⟩H−1=⟨Δ​μn+1,ϕn+1−ϕn⟩H−1.\left\langle\frac{\phi^{n+1}-\phi^{n}}{\Delta t},\phi^{n+1}-\phi^{n}\right\rangle_{H^{-1}}=\langle\Delta\mu^{n+1},\phi^{n+1}-\phi^{n}\rangle_{H^{-1}}.

Using periodicity and the identity

⟨Δ​v,w⟩H−1=−⟨v,w⟩L2,\langle\Delta v,w\rangle_{H^{-1}}=-\langle v,w\rangle_{L^{2}},

we obtain

1Δ​t​‖ϕn+1−ϕn‖H−12=−⟨μn+1,ϕn+1−ϕn⟩L2.\frac{1}{\Delta t}\|\phi^{n+1}-\phi^{n}\|_{H^{-1}}^{2}=-\langle\mu^{n+1},\phi^{n+1}-\phi^{n}\rangle_{L^{2}}. (2.3)

Since EM+E_{M}^{+} is convex,

EM+​(ϕn+1)−EM+​(ϕn)≤⟨δ​EM+​(ϕn+1),ϕn+1−ϕn⟩L2.E_{M}^{+}(\phi^{n+1})-E_{M}^{+}(\phi^{n})\leq\left\langle\delta E_{M}^{+}(\phi^{n+1}),\phi^{n+1}-\phi^{n}\right\rangle_{L^{2}}. (2.4)

Since EM−E_{M}^{-} is concave,

EM−​(ϕn+1)−EM−​(ϕn)≤⟨δ​EM−​(ϕn),ϕn+1−ϕn⟩L2.E_{M}^{-}(\phi^{n+1})-E_{M}^{-}(\phi^{n})\leq\left\langle\delta E_{M}^{-}(\phi^{n}),\phi^{n+1}-\phi^{n}\right\rangle_{L^{2}}. (2.5)

Adding (2.4) and (2.5) yields

EM​(ϕn+1)−EM​(ϕn)≤⟨δ​EM+​(ϕn+1)+δ​EM−​(ϕn),ϕn+1−ϕn⟩L2.E_{M}(\phi^{n+1})-E_{M}(\phi^{n})\leq\left\langle\delta E_{M}^{+}(\phi^{n+1})+\delta E_{M}^{-}(\phi^{n}),\phi^{n+1}-\phi^{n}\right\rangle_{L^{2}}.

Using the definition of μn+1\mu^{n+1} from (2.2),

EM​(ϕn+1)−EM​(ϕn)≤⟨μn+1,ϕn+1−ϕn⟩L2.E_{M}(\phi^{n+1})-E_{M}(\phi^{n})\leq\langle\mu^{n+1},\phi^{n+1}-\phi^{n}\rangle_{L^{2}}.

Substituting identity (2.3),

EM​(ϕn+1)−EM​(ϕn)≤−1Δ​t​‖ϕn+1−ϕn‖H−12.E_{M}(\phi^{n+1})-E_{M}(\phi^{n})\leq-\frac{1}{\Delta t}\|\phi^{n+1}-\phi^{n}\|_{H^{-1}}^{2}.

Therefore,

EM​(ϕn+1)+1Δ​t​‖ϕn+1−ϕn‖H−12≤EM​(ϕn).E_{M}(\phi^{n+1})+\frac{1}{\Delta t}\|\phi^{n+1}-\phi^{n}\|_{H^{-1}}^{2}\leq E_{M}(\phi^{n}).

∎

Remark 3.

In practical computations, one typically observes |ϕ|≤M|\phi|\leq M [19, 21, 22], so that

FM​(ϕ)=14​ϕ4F_{M}(\phi)=\frac{1}{4}\phi^{4}

throughout the simulation. Thus the truncated formulation serves only as a technical device ensuring global concavity and rigorous unconditional energy stability.

5 Computational Stability Analysis

5.1 Single Run: Crystal Growth from Seed

To illustrate the dynamics of the proposed scheme, we first present a single simulation of the PFC equation initialized with the standard seed configuration of Glasner–Orizaga [19]. The simulation is performed on a 256×256256\times 256 grid with r=0.5r=0.5, Δ​t=0.01\Delta t=0.01, and a=0.30a=0.30, a value notably below the classical threshold a≥2a\geq 2, demonstrating that energy-stable and physically correct simulations are achievable well below this bound. Figure 1 shows snapshots of the atomistic density field at t=0,10,20,40t=0,10,20,40, demonstrating the progressive growth of a hexagonal crystal lattice from the initial seed. Figure 2 shows the corresponding free energy as a function of time, confirming monotonic energy dissipation throughout the simulation.

5.2 GPU-Accelerated Parallel Simulations

To further demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed framework, we exploit GPU parallelism to execute twenty independent PFC simulations simultaneously, each with a different value of the splitting parameter a∈[1.00,2.00]a\in[1.00,2.00]. This is motivated in part by recent advances in GPU-parallelized scientific computing, in particular, Chowdhury and Pérez-Ríos [29] demonstrated the effectiveness of GPU-parallelized MATLAB for large-scale parameter sweeps in atom-ion dynamics, achieving significant speedups over CPU-based implementations. The present work adopts a similar philosophy. As shown in Figure 3, all twenty simulations are energy-stable, confirming that values of aa significantly below the classical threshold a≥2a\geq 2 yield physically correct solutions. A GPU speedup of 18.42×18.42\times over the sequential CPU baseline is observed.

5.3 Neutral Stability Curve

While Theorem 2 establishes that a≥LMa\geq L_{M} is sufficient for unconditional energy stability, this condition is not sharp in practice. To characterize the practical stability boundary, we derive a semi-analytical neutral stability curve from a dominant-mode energy balance.

From the discrete energy law established in Theorem 2, the neutral stability transition occurs when EM​(ϕn+1)=EM​(ϕn)E_{M}(\phi^{n+1})=E_{M}(\phi^{n}), that is, when the dissipative terms and the nonlinear remainder are in exact balance. To make this condition tractable, we invoke a dominant-mode reduction: we project the balance onto the dominant Fourier mode |𝐤|2=2|\mathbf{k}|^{2}=2, evaluate the nonlinearity at its bulk-phase value f′′=FM′′​(ϕ)|ϕ=1=2f^{\prime\prime}=F_{M}^{\prime\prime}(\phi)|_{\phi=1}=2, and collect terms in aa. This yields the quadratic condition

a⁡(1+Δ​t​|𝐤|6+Δ​t​a​|𝐤|2)=f′′​Δ​t​|𝐤|2.a\left(1+\Delta t\,|\mathbf{k}|^{6}+\Delta t\,a\,|\mathbf{k}|^{2}\right)=f^{\prime\prime}\,\Delta t\,|\mathbf{k}|^{2}.

Solving for the positive root gives the analytical neutral curve:

aneutral​(Δ​t)=−(1+Δ​t​|𝐤|6)+(1+Δ​t​|𝐤|6)2+4​Δ​t2​|𝐤|4​f′′2​Δ​t​|𝐤|2,a_{\mathrm{neutral}}(\Delta t)=\frac{-(1+\Delta t\,|\mathbf{k}|^{6})+\sqrt{(1+\Delta t\,|\mathbf{k}|^{6})^{2}+4\,\Delta t^{2}\,|\mathbf{k}|^{4}\,f^{\prime\prime}}}{2\,\Delta t\,|\mathbf{k}|^{2}}, (7)

which contains no free parameters under this closure. As Δ​t→0\Delta t\to 0, aneutral→0a_{\mathrm{neutral}}\to 0, consistent with the explicit CFL-type behavior observed numerically. For large Δ​t\Delta t, aneutrala_{\mathrm{neutral}} grows monotonically, reflecting increased stabilization requirements. The curve lies well below the classical bound a≥2a\geq 2 over the entire tested range Δ​t∈[0.01,2]\Delta t\in[0.01,2], confirming that the standard condition is not sharp in practice. Any choice satisfying a≥aneutral​(Δ​t)a\geq a_{\mathrm{neutral}}(\Delta t) is consistently observed to yield energy-stable simulations, providing a practical and conservative guideline for parameter selection.

5.4 GPU-Accelerated Stability Map

To verify the neutral stability curve (7) computationally, we perform a systematic parameter sweep over (a,Δ​t)∈[0,0.4]×[0.01,2](a,\Delta t)\in[0,0.4]\times[0.01,2] using 40,000 independent GPU-accelerated PFC simulations on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU. Each simulation is initialized with the standard seed configuration in [19] on a 64×6464\times 64 grid with r=0.5r=0.5. To ensure a fair and rigorous comparison across all parameter pairs, each simulation is advanced for a fixed number of time steps given by

Nsteps=⌊TΔ​tmin⌋=⌊140.01⌋=1400,N_{\mathrm{steps}}=\left\lfloor\frac{T}{\Delta t_{\min}}\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor\frac{14}{0.01}\right\rfloor=1400,

regardless of the value of Δ​t\Delta t. A simulation is classified as stable if the discrete free energy satisfies E⁡(ϕNsteps)<E⁡(ϕ0)E(\phi^{N_{\mathrm{steps}}})<E(\phi^{0}), a criterion verified to correspond to physically meaningful solutions in representative cases.

Figure 5 shows the semi-analytical neutral stability curve (7) overlaid against the computational stability boundary extracted from the stability map of Figure 4. The neutral curve lies above the computational boundary throughout the tested range, confirming its conservative but reliable character as a practical guideline for parameter selection. Notably, the neutral curve remains substantially below the classical sufficient condition a≥2a\geq 2 of Eyre [1] across the entire tested range Δ​t∈[0.01,2]\Delta t\in[0.01,2], demonstrating that the classical bound is significantly more conservative than necessary in practice.

This approach is broadly applicable to any phase-field or gradient flow model requiring systematic parameter exploration. The 40,000 GPU-accelerated simulations presented here demonstrate that computational stability maps, previously impractical due to cost, are now accessible on consumer hardware, opening new avenues for parameter sensitivity analysis in materials science, crystal growth modeling, and beyond.

Remark 4 (Robustness of the Stability Map).

The computational stability map presented in Figure 4 was obtained using the seed configuration of [19]. Additional tests with random initial conditions ϕ0=0.01​η\phi^{0}=0.01\,\eta, η∼𝒩⁡(0,1)\eta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1), yielded near-identical stability boundaries, suggesting that the stability boundary is an intrinsic property of the CS scheme rather than a consequence of the choice of initial condition.

6 Accuracy Analysis: Influence of the Splitting Parameter

The computational stability map of Figure 4 demonstrates that energy-stable simulations are achievable for values of aa significantly below the classical threshold a≥2a\geq 2. A natural question is whether reducing aa within the stable region affects the accuracy of the numerical solution. We investigate this systematically by computing L2L^{2} errors relative to a reference solution obtained with a=2a=2 and Δ​t=10−5\Delta t=10^{-5} on a 256×256256\times 256 grid up to T=1T=1, using the standard seed initial condition in [19].

Figure 6 shows the L2L^{2} error as a function of Δ​t\Delta t for five values of a∈{0.1,0.5,1.0,1.5,2.0}a\in\{0.1,0.5,1.0,1.5,2.0\}. All curves exhibit first-order 𝒪⁡(Δ​t)\mathcal{O}(\Delta t) convergence, consistent with the first-order temporal discretization. Crucially, smaller values of aa consistently yield lower L2L^{2} errors for the same Δ​t\Delta t. This demonstrates that selecting aa close to aneutral​(Δ​t)a_{\mathrm{neutral}}(\Delta t), rather than the conservative choice a=2a=2, improves accuracy while maintaining energy stability, providing a practical guideline for parameter selection.

7 Numerical Simulations: 2D

7.1 Lamellar Phase: Stripe Formation

To further demonstrate the capabilities of the proposed scheme beyond the seed configuration, we present long-time simulations initialized with a random initial condition ϕ0=0.01​η\phi^{0}=0.01\,\eta, η∼𝒩⁡(0,1)\eta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1), on a 256×256256\times 256 grid with r=0.5r=0.5, Δ​t=0.01\Delta t=0.01, and a=0.5a=0.5. This configuration tests the ability of the method to naturally develop labyrinthine stripe patterns from an unstructured initial state, without any prescribed geometry. Figure 7 shows snapshots at t=5t=5, t=40t=40, and t=1000t=1000, illustrating the progressive formation and coarsening of the lamellar microstructure. Figure 8 shows the corresponding free energy, which decreases monotonically and reaches a well-defined plateau near t=500t=500, confirming that the solution has reached a near-equilibrium state.

7.2 Hexagonal Phase

We next consider a mean-field initial condition ϕ0=0.01​η+0.27\phi^{0}=0.01\,\eta+0.27, η∼𝒩⁡(0,1)\eta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1), which favors the formation of hexagonal dot patterns. Figure 9 shows snapshots at t=10t=10, t=50t=50, and t=1000t=1000, demonstrating the progressive development of the hexagonal microstructure. Figure 10 shows the corresponding free energy, which decreases monotonically throughout, consistent with Theorem 2.

7.3 Polycrystalline Growth and Grain Boundary Dynamics

To demonstrate the ability of the proposed scheme to capture polycrystalline growth and grain boundary dynamics, we initialize three seed crystals with different orientations within a 256×256256\times 256 computational domain with r=0.25r=0.25, q=0.66q=0.66, Δ​t=0.01\Delta t=0.01, and a=0.5a=0.5. Each seed is initialized using the standard crystal nucleus configuration  [19] with a distinct rotation angle, inducing crystallographic misorientation between the growing grains. As the three crystals grow and impinge upon one another, well-defined grain boundaries and dislocation defects emerge at the interfaces, as shown in Figure 11. The free energy decreases monotonically throughout, consistent with Theorem 2.

7.4 Quantitative Grain Boundary Characterization

Figure 11 qualitatively demonstrates the emergence of grain boundaries between three misoriented crystal seeds. Next, we quantify the coarsening dynamics using four types of diagnostic approaches, which were computed directly from the simulation: the topological defect count Nd​(t)N_{d}(t), the grain boundary length LG​B​(t)L_{GB}(t), the grain boundary excess free energy EG​B​(t)E_{GB}(t), and the crystallized area fraction X⁡(t)X(t). Results from this anlaysis is presented in Figure 12.

Topological defect count: We locate the local extrema of u⁡(𝐱,t)u(\mathbf{x},t), corresponding to the atomic lattice sites, and construct a Delaunay triangulation over this point set. In a defect-free triangular lattice every interior site has coordination number six, so

Nd(t)=∑i∈Ωint[zi(t)≠6],N_{d}(t)\;=\;\sum_{i\,\in\,\Omega_{\mathrm{int}}}\mathbb{1}\!\left[\,z_{i}(t)\neq 6\,\right], (8)

where zi​(t)z_{i}(t) denotes the Delaunay coordination number of site ii, 𝟙​[⋅]\mathbb{1}[\cdot] is the indicator function that equals 11 if the enclosed condition is satisfied and 00 otherwise, and Ωint\Omega_{\mathrm{int}} consists of all lattice sites located at least one lattice spacing away from the domain boundary.

We emphasize that Nd​(t)N_{d}(t) aggregates all anomalous-coordination sites across the domain; meaning, (8) captures deviations from ideal coordination number equal to six. Comparing with Figure 11, such deviations appear at the crystal/liquid interfaces (e.g., tt=100.0), and grain boundary regions (e.g., tt=500.0).

The results from Nd​(t)N_{d}(t) v.s. tt analysis is presented in the top-left panel of Figure 12. Broadly, this plot shows three distinct regions: An initial rise between 0≤t≤2000\leq t\leq 200, monotonic decrease from t≈200t\approx 200 to 400400, and a near steady-state till the end of simulation, i.e., t=500t=500. The initial rise to t≈200t\approx 200 corresponds to increasing fraction of anomalously coordinated atoms at crystal/liquid interface during growth (while largely surrounded by the liquid phase), and those at the grain boundaries formed by the impinging crystallites (e.g., see panel corresponding to t=100t=100 in Figure 11. Next, as the liquid is continually consumed by growing crystals, the anomalously coordinated atom population is increasingly dominated by those at the grain boundaries. For example, the t=200t=200 snapshot indicated that the microstructure is dominated by grain boundaries in the second stage. Interestingly, it appears that such grain boundary atoms were in smaller quantity than those at the crystal/liquid interface. Furthermore, our analysis suggested that microstructure did not stop evolving even after complete crystallization, e.g. to t=400t=400. (Crystallization kinetics captured from our simulations will be discussed latter). However, beyond this point, the grain boundaries appear to be "locked in" an equilibrium state, which is reflected as a steady state in the plot.

Interface length: We further characterized these interfaces by computing local orientation, θ⁡(𝐱,t)\theta(\mathbf{x},t), as a function of time. This quantity was obtained from the dominant spectral peak of a sliding-window Fourier transform of u⁡(𝐱,t)u(\mathbf{x},t), taken modulo 60∘60^{\circ}. Writing ζ⁡(𝐱,t)=exp⁡[i​ 6​θ​(𝐱,t)]\zeta(\mathbf{x},t)=\exp[i\,6\,\theta(\mathbf{x},t)] to avoid the wrap-around artifact of this periodicity,

LG​B​(t)=∫ΩH⁡(16​|∇ζ​(𝐱,t)|−η)​𝑑𝐱,L_{GB}(t)\;=\;\int_{\Omega}H\!\left(\,\tfrac{1}{6}\left|\nabla\zeta(\mathbf{x},t)\right|-\eta\,\right)\,d\mathbf{x}, (9)

with η=5∘\eta=5^{\circ} per grid step, is a coarse but reproducible proxy for the grain-boundary arclength.

The top-right plot in Figure 12 shows the result of our analysis. We find that the interfacial length steadily increases till t≈250t\approx 250, and, subsequently, acquires a steady-state value. A small peak was also noted within 200≤t≤300200\leq t\leq 300. It was either caused by the transition to a grain boundary dominated microstructure or is an imprint of the numerical procedure employed in this analysis. Notwithstanding, the initial rise in LG​B​(t)L_{GB}(t) contains contributions from the increasing circumference of the growing crystals and the proto grain boundaries, e.g. see snapshots corresponding to t=50t=50 and 100100 in Figure 11. On the other hand, the steady-state is primarily dominated by the grain boundaries after t≈300t\approx 300.

Interfacial excess free energy: With bulk reference fbulk​(t)=median𝐱∈Ω​f​(u⁡(𝐱,t))f_{\mathrm{bulk}}(t)=\mathrm{median}_{\mathbf{x}\in\Omega}\,f(u(\mathbf{x},t)),

EG​B​(t)=∫Ω[f⁡(u⁡(𝐱,t))−fbulk​(t)]+​𝑑𝐱E_{GB}(t)\;=\;\int_{\Omega}\Big[\,f\big(u(\mathbf{x},t)\big)-f_{\mathrm{bulk}}(t)\,\Big]^{+}\,d\mathbf{x} (10)

computes the excess free energy of interfaces, and this approach was inspired by Cahn-Hilliard-based formulations[4, 30, 31, 32]. Plot in the bottom-right panel of Figure 12 depicts the evolution of fbulk​(t)f_{\mathrm{bulk}}(t), and it trends comparable to LG​B​(t)L_{GB}(t) (top-right panel): a monotonic rise followed by steady state. Therefore, the initial rise correspond to excess energies of crystal/liquid and grain boundary interfaces, while the steady-state reflects contributions from the interfaces formed by the misoriented crystals,i.e., grain boundaries.

Crystallization kinetics: Lastly, we interrogated the crystallization kinetics by measuring the crystallized fraction (X⁡(t)∈[0,1]X(t)\in[0,1] ) as function of time - bottom-right panel in Figure 12. We note that trend in X⁡(t)X(t) is comparable to LG​B​(t)L_{GB}(t) (top-right panel) and EG​B​(t)E_{GB}(t) (bottom-left panel), and that full crystallization (OPENX⁡(t)=1)X(t)=1)) was achieved around t≈250t\approx 250. The latter corresponded to microstructure dominated by grain boundary interfaces. Next, we quantified crystallization kinetics by fitting the Johnson–Mehl–Avrami–Kolmogorov (JMAK) equation to the simulation data [33, 34]:

X⁡(t)=1−exp⁡(−k​tn)X(t)=1-\exp(-kt^{n}) (11)

where, kk is a measure of the speed of liquid→\xrightarrow{}solid (crystal) transformation, and the exponent nn signifies the dimensionality of transformation. n≈3n\approx 3 corresponds to three dimensional volumetric transformation, while n≈2n\approx 2 points to a transformation mechanism that is dominated by interfaces [33, 34, 35]. The fitting results presented in the plot, and, importantly, we find that n=1.79n=1.79 - close to a value of two. This further confirms that the microstructural evolution observed in Figure 11 is dominated by interfaces; first by the crystal/liquid, and, after complete crystallization, by crystal/crystal grain boundary interfaces.

Having established the scheme’s ability to capture and quantify mesoscale polycrystalline dynamics, we next examine its performance at the atomistic length scales for which the PFC framework was originally intended.

7.5 Atomistic Resolution: High-Resolution Crystal Growth

The PFC equation was originally derived to model microstructure evolution at atomic length scales [2, 3]. As demonstrated in the comprehensive review of Gránásy et al. [36], phase-field crystal models require sufficient spatial resolution to faithfully capture crystal nucleation, grain boundary dynamics, and microstructure evolution at the molecular scale, phenomena that are inaccessible at coarser resolutions. To demonstrate the ability of the proposed scheme to resolve such dynamics, we consider high-resolution simulations on grids up to 2048×20482048\times 2048, enabling thousands of individual crystalline sites to be resolved simultaneously and directly capturing the atomistic lattice structure characteristic of the model.

To further assess the behavior of the scheme in a strongly under-resolved stability regime, we perform a simulation on a 2048×20482048\times 2048 grid using a=0.25a=0.25, well below the classical convex-splitting threshold a≥2a\geq 2. Despite this, the computation remains stable throughout and accurately captures the evolution of thousands of crystalline sites across the domain. Figure 13 shows the resulting dynamics, illustrating the formation and coarsening of a hexagonal crystal lattice from a single seed.

These large-scale simulations highlight that the relaxed stability conditions identified in the computational analysis remain effective in practice for long-time, high-resolution atomistic dynamics. This sets the stage for extending the framework to fully three-dimensional simulations in the following section.

8 Three-Dimensional Simulations and GPU Scalability

8.1 GPU Scalability

GPU acceleration for spectral phase-field models was previously benchmarked in [21], where an NVIDIA RTX 2060 GPU achieved a conservative 8×8\times speedup over an Intel Core i9 CPU baseline for the Cahn–Hilliard equation on large-scale problems involving 2563256^{3} grids. GPU-accelerated spectral methods for PDEs have also been explored in the context of tensor product operations [20] and thin-film equations [37], demonstrating the broad applicability of GPU acceleration for spectral phase-field computations. In the present work, GPU parallelism is further exploited to perform large-scale parameter sweeps involving 40,000 independent PFC simulations, motivated by recent advances in GPU-parallelized scientific computing [29].

To illustrate the three-dimensional capabilities of the proposed scheme, we present a benchmark simulation using the standard seed initial condition of [19] extended to three spatial dimensions. The benchmark is designed to reflect realistic computational conditions: a main script calls the solver, timing begins at initialization, and concludes only once the full three-dimensional solution is computed and available for visualization and exploration. All simulations use r=0.5r=0.5, Δ​t=0.01\Delta t=0.01, a=0.5a=0.5, and T=100T=100, corresponding to 10,000 time steps at resolutions of 1283128^{3} and 2563256^{3}, representing approximately 2 million and 16 million degrees of freedom per time step, respectively. Figure 14 shows the isosurface visualization and internal cross-sections at the center of the domain, revealing the three-dimensional crystal microstructure. Mass is conserved to machine precision throughout.

Building on this foundation, we benchmark three GPU configurations for the PFC equation using the same seed initial condition with Δ​t=0.01\Delta t=0.01 and T=100T=100. Table 1 summarizes the wall-clock times and relative speedups for grid resolutions of 1283128^{3} and 2563256^{3}.

The proposed CS scheme is benchmarked on modern NVIDIA Blackwell GPU architectures to demonstrate scalability for large-scale 3D PFC simulations. Table 1 reports wall-clock times for consumer and professional-grade GPUs. Given the 8×8\times speedup of the RTX 2060 over a CPU baseline [21], the RTX 5090 desktop achieves an effective speedup of approximately 70×70\times over CPU, approaching the 80×80\times reported for the professional NVIDIA A100 in [21]. The professional-grade RTX PRO 6000 reaches 94×94\times, confirming that the gap between consumer and professional hardware is closing for phase-field workloads. These results demonstrate that large-scale 3D PFC simulations are now accessible on consumer hardware without HPC infrastructure.

The RTX 5090 laptop achieves an effective speedup of approximately 40×40\times over CPU, comparable to the professional A6000 reported in [21], demonstrating that high-resolution 3D PFC simulations are now feasible on portable consumer hardware.

8.2 3D GPU-Accelerated PFC Morphologies

The proposed scheme naturally captures a rich variety of three-dimensional microstructures depending solely on the mean-field value of the initial condition, without requiring prescribed seed configurations. Specifically, we consider initial conditions of the form

ϕ0=0.01​η+ϕ¯,η∼𝒩⁡(0,1),\phi^{0}=0.01\,\eta+\bar{\phi},\qquad\eta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1),

where ϕ¯\bar{\phi} denotes the mean density. By varying ϕ¯\bar{\phi}, three qualitatively distinct phases emerge naturally from random initial conditions, demonstrating the morphological versatility of the convex splitting spectral framework. All simulations are performed on 2563256^{3} and 5123512^{3} grids with r=0.5r=0.5, Δ​t=0.01\Delta t=0.01, a=1.0a=1.0, and T=1000T=1000 using the consumer-grade RTX 5090 desktop GPU.

8.2.1 Lamellar Phase (ϕ¯=0\bar{\phi}=0)

Setting ϕ¯=0\bar{\phi}=0, the system develops a three-dimensional labyrinthine stripe pattern distributed throughout the computational domain. The fine-scale structure reflects the atomistic length scale of the PFC equation, producing richly textured microstructure distinct from the coarser interfaces observed in classical phase-field models. Figure 15 shows the isosurface at T=1000T=1000, and Figure 16 shows the corresponding free energy.

8.2.2 Spherical Phase (ϕ¯=0.35\bar{\phi}=0.35)

Setting ϕ¯=0.35\bar{\phi}=0.35, the higher mean density favors the formation of isolated spherical microdomains distributed throughout the computational domain. Unlike the classical Cahn–Hilliard equation where spherical domains undergo Ostwald ripening, the PFC equation stabilizes the spherical phase through its atomistic structure, maintaining well-defined spherical microdomains throughout the simulation. Figure 17 shows the isosurface at T=1000T=1000, and Figure 18 shows the corresponding free energy, which decreases monotonically consistent with Theorem 2.

8.2.3 Hexagonal Cylindrical Phase (ϕ¯=0.25\bar{\phi}=0.25)

To demonstrate the scalability of the proposed framework, we consider an intermediate mean density ϕ¯=0.25\bar{\phi}=0.25, which produces a hexagonal cylindrical phase characterized by interconnected tubular microstructures. To fully capture the atomistic activity at this scale, we scale up to a 5123512^{3} grid, corresponding to approximately 134 million degrees of freedom. This resolution reveals the rich three-dimensional tubular network that emerges from the PFC dynamics, providing a stringent test of both the energy stability and the GPU scalability of the proposed scheme. Figure 19 shows the isosurface and Figure 20 shows the corresponding free energy.

Remark 5 (GPU Acceleration).

Each 2563256^{3} simulation presented above runs to T=1000T=1000 with Δ​t=0.01\Delta t=0.01, corresponding to 100,000 time steps on a grid of 2563=16,777,216256^{3}=16{,}777{,}216 degrees of freedom, over 16 million unknowns updated at every step. On a CPU baseline, such a computation would require approximately 94×70≈6,58094\times 70\approx 6{,}580 minutes, or over 4.5 days, on a single core without HPC infrastructure. All of this was completed in under 94 minutes on a single consumer NVIDIA RTX 5090 desktop GPU.

Remark 6 (GPU Acceleration at 5123512^{3}).

The 5123512^{3} hexagonal cylindrical phase simulation runs to T=1000T=1000 with Δ​t=0.01\Delta t=0.01, corresponding to 100,000 time steps on a grid of 5123=134,217,728512^{3}=134{,}217{,}728 degrees of freedom. On a CPU baseline, such a computation would require approximately 18 days on a single core without HPC infrastructure. On a single consumer GPU, this simulation completed in under 6 hours.

Remark 7.

Every simulation in this work, including the 40,000 parametric sweeps and the three-dimensional computations, is executed strictly in native double-precision (FP64). As demonstrated in [21], single-precision (FP32) introduces an unphysical mass leakage of 𝒪⁡(10−4)\mathcal{O}(10^{-4}) over long temporal scales. Maintaining full FP64 precision across all GPU configurations guarantees mass conservation to machine precision (𝒪⁡(10−14)\mathcal{O}(10^{-14})), ensuring that the reported speedups reflect genuine algorithmic efficiency under uncompromised physical rigor.

8.3 Asymptotic Energy Behavior: Lamellar Phase at T=10,000T=10{,}000 (10610^{6} Time Steps)

To demonstrate the long-time robustness of the proposed scheme, we extend the lamellar phase simulation to T=10,000T=10{,}000 with Δ​t=0.01\Delta t=0.01, corresponding to 10610^{6} time steps on a 2563256^{3} grid with ϕ¯=0\bar{\phi}=0, r=0.5r=0.5, with a=1.0a=1.0, a value below the classical threshold a≥2a\geq 2 but satisfying the derived neutral stability curve (7). Figure 21 shows the isosurface of the lamellar phase at T=10,000T=10{,}000, revealing well-developed three-dimensional lamellar stripes. Figure 22 shows the corresponding free energy on a log scale, demonstrating monotonic dissipation and convergence to a well-defined asymptotic plateau, demonstrating monotonic dissipation and convergence toward an asymptotically stable energy plateau. Mass is conserved to machine precision throughout all 10610^{6} time steps.

9 Conclusions

We have presented an efficient Fourier spectral method based on the convex splitting framework for the phase field crystal equation. The proposed first-order scheme is unconditionally energy stable, conserves mass to machine precision, and admits a closed-form spectral update requiring a few lines of MATLAB code.

A central contribution of this work is a computational stability analysis of the splitting parameter aa, performed via GPU-accelerated parameter sweeps involving 40,000 independent PFC simulations. Our results demonstrate that the classical sufficient condition a≥2a\geq 2 is not sharp: a semi-analytical neutral stability curve derived from a dominant-mode energy balance provides a closed-form characterization of the practical stability boundary, lying well below the classical bound. Moreover, accuracy analysis across multiple initial conditions consistently demonstrates that smaller values of aa within the stable region yield lower L2L^{2} errors while preserving the energy decreasing property, providing a practical guideline for parameter selection.

Two-dimensional simulations on 256×256256\times 256 and high resolution grids demonstrate the efficiency and morphological richness of the proposed framework, including crystal growth from a single seed, lamellar and hexagonal structures emerging from random initial conditions, and grain boundary dynamics from polycrystalline configurations. Three-dimensional GPU-accelerated simulations at resolutions of 1283128^{3}, 2563256^{3}, and 5123512^{3} on a single consumer GPU further demonstrate the scalability of the method. Three qualitatively distinct phases emerge naturally in three dimensions from random initial conditions by varying only the mean density ϕ¯\bar{\phi}, suggesting that the proposed framework is robust for exploring the rich morphological landscape of the PFC equation in three spatial dimensions. Long-time three-dimensional simulations up to T=10,000T=10,000 (10610^{6} time steps) further demonstrate robustness in the relaxed stability regime predicted by the derived neutral stability curve. These large-scale FP64 computations maintain monotonic energy dissipation and mass conservation to machine precision throughout the entire evolution.

Future work includes the extension of this framework to second-order temporal schemes via BDF2–CS and IMEX methods [19, 5, 38], noting that the first-order temporal discretization adopted in the present work is a deliberate methodological choice rather than a limitation of the underlying convex splitting framework: as demonstrated in [19], second-order accuracy via BDF2–CS is readily achievable. We note, however, that the practical stability threshold for aa identified here is specific to the first-order temporal discretization analyzed in this work; characterizing how this threshold shifts under BDF2–CS or other higher-order schemes is a natural and nontrivial direction for future investigation, adaptive time-stepping strategies guided by the neutral stability curve, and applications to related phase-field models including the block copolymer systems [7, 9, 10]. Extensions to thin-film equations with similar interfacial dynamics also represent a natural direction for future investigation [39, 40, 41]. Moreover, we plan to extend this framework to higher-order phase-field crystal models, including the eighth-order PFC equation [42, 43], the Lifshitz–Petrich model for quasicrystalline structures [44, 45], which captures additional crystallographic detail beyond the standard sixth-order formulation.

The quantitative grain boundary characterization introduced in Section 7.4 is directly relevant to materials science applications, and we plan to pursue further work in this direction, including more detailed defect and grain-growth statistics. Our GPU-based implementation of PFC further paves way for coupling with atomistic simulations, e.g., using ab initio and classical molecular dynamics (MD). These MD-based techniques are capable of describing complex structures, e.g., multi-phase interfaces, organic-inorganic molecules, and the like, and their time-evolution through well-established mathematical formulations and interatomic potentials [46, 47, 48, 32, 35]. However, they are limited to probing mechanisms at short time scales, e.g., within pico-nanoseconds, only. On the other hand, PFC simulations can extend to microseconds, and, therefore, can probe physical phenomenon in materials that may be inaccessible to MD. A possible pathway for such multi-temporal coupling is using MD simulations to inform parameters in the energy functional, e.g. rr and aa in equations. 3 and 5, which is crucial for PFC simulations. Recent developments in Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) may allow such information transfer, where PINNs can be trained on MD data while being constrained with a physics-based mathematical function [48, 49].

The GPU-parallelized parameter sweep strategy adopted here, motivated by recent advances in atom-ion dynamics [29], is broadly applicable to phase-field and gradient-flow models requiring systematic stability or sensitivity analysis across large parameter spaces. Many modern numerical frameworks, including higher-order convex splitting, SAV, and IMEX-type schemes, introduce stabilization or splitting parameters whose practical stability regions invite further computational exploration. The present GPU-parallel stability-map methodology provides a scalable and reproducible framework for systematically exploring such parameter landscapes through large-scale PDE simulations on consumer hardware.
